intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Hoxha-Aliu syndrome (HXAL) is caused by homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the ERI1 gene (608739) on chromosome 8p23.1.

checks.claim: Hoxha-Aliu syndrome (HXAL) is caused by homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the ERI1 gene.

paragraphs.text: Hoxha-Aliu syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its features include mild intellectual disability and anomalies of the digits. Guo et al. paragraphs.text: Szot et al. (2021) reported a girl (F5.II.1). She had a perimembranous ventricular septal defect and pulmonary vein stenosis. Her limb findings were reduction defects, namely a transverse terminal limb reduction of the right hand with a rudimentary fifth digit, together with absent toes, absent or hypoplastic nails, and syndactyly. She also had microcephaly, global developmental delay, and autism. Her craniofacial features included brachycephaly, a flat occiput, bitemporal narrowing, a small nose with a normal philtrum, and cupped, prominent ears. She had bilateral inguinal hernias. She had no vertebral or renal anomalies.

paragraphs.text: Choucair et al. (2017) performed chromosomal microarray analysis in a boy with intellectual disability, synpolydactyly, and cardiac malformations who was born to consanguineous parents. They found a homozygous deletion at 8p23.1 that contained the microRNA miR-4660 and the ERI1 and MFHAS1 genes. The authors noted that ERI1 is a ribonuclease involved in RNA metabolism and is required for correct skeletal patterning because it defines HOXC8 expression. They discussed whether loss of ERI1 might contribute to the patient's limb abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: In a girl (F5.II.1) with limb reduction defects and cardiac anomalies, Szot et al. (2021) found a homozygous loss-of-function variant in the ERI1 gene (c.514C-T, gln172-to-ter, Q172X). The same girl was also homozygous for a missense variant in the KYNU gene (glu206-to-lys, E206K), which she had inherited from asymptomatic parents. This KYNU variant caused only mild NAD deficiency in a yeast assay. The authors noted that ERI1 had previously been found in a homozygous microdeletion, together with MFHAS1, in a patient with limb and cardiac abnormalities similar to hers. They suggested that the ERI1 variant may partly explain her limb and cardiac anomalies, but noted that the functional link between ERI1 mutation and these defects remained to be assessed.

paragraphs.text: Guo et al. (2023) described a phenotypic dichotomy in individuals with biallelic ERI1 variants. Five affected individuals with missense variants had severe spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia. Individuals with biallelic null variants did not have it, and instead showed mild intellectual disability and digital anomalies. The missense variants abolished the exoribonuclease activity of ERI1. This led to defective trimming of the 3-prime end of 5.8S rRNA and reduced degradation of replication-dependent histone mRNAs. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from affected individuals showed impaired in vitro chondrogenesis and downregulation of genes that regulate skeletal patterning. The authors proposed a model in which, within recessive genotypes, missense alleles have a more severe effect than null alleles.

paragraphs.text: Szot et al. (2021) reported a girl (F5.II.1) with limb reduction defects, a perimembranous ventricular septal defect, pulmonary vein stenosis, microcephaly, global developmental delay, and autism. She was homozygous for a c.514C-T transition (NM_153332.4) in the ERI1 gene, which results in a gln172-to-ter (Q172X) substitution and is predicted to cause loss of function. She was also homozygous for a KYNU missense variant (E206K), which caused only mild NAD deficiency in a yeast assay. The authors suggested that the ERI1 variant may partly explain her limb and cardiac anomalies, but noted that its functional link to these defects remained to be assessed.
